conflicts.issue: Reallocating Unspent Low-Income Homeowner Relief Grant Funds to Eviction Diversion
conflicts.summary: Officials debated a County proposal to bridge the $320,000 eviction diversion shortfall by tapping unspent funds in the joint $1.2M Low-Income Homeowner Relief Grant program ($700K County / $500K City).
conflicts.side_a_position: Consider reallocating underutilized Low-Income Homeowner Relief Grant dollars to stabilize eviction diversion immediately.
side_a_arguments: Roughly $1.2M was allocated to homeowner relief with only ~$400K+ spent across two years, leaving idle funds on the table while eviction diversion runs out of money this month.
Moving unused ('lazy') funds in an acute housing crisis is sound fiscal practice and does not preclude replenishing homeowner relief later if needed.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not pit low-income homeowners against renters or reduce homeowner relief funds ahead of the upcoming property tax revaluation; fix application barriers instead.
side_b_arguments: Cutting homeowner relief ahead of next year's property tax revaluation risks harming vulnerable homeowners; the program is underutilized because the application process is clunky and needs streamlining.
Other funding sources should be identified to cover the $320,000 gap and $1.3M annual need.
conflicts.resolution: Mayor Leonardo Williams agreed to meet with BOCC Chair Nida Allam and both the City and County Managers to identify the best funding mechanism without an immediate vote.

conflicts.issue: Homelessness Interventions, Shelter Capacity vs. Rapid Rehousing, and Eviction Diversion Accountability
conflicts.summary: Commissioners and Council members debated how to balance limited funding between emergency/non-congregate shelter and rapid rehousing, how to track bond-funded affordable housing set-asides, and whether eviction diversion rental assistance requires stronger post-aid outcome tracking.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize immediate mid-year replenishment, non-traditional shelter (pallet homes, safe parking, day centers), and stronger Continuum of Care tracking for special populations.
side_a_arguments: DSS eviction diversion ($45,184 remaining) and Open Doors ($14,786 remaining) funds will run out before spring, and coordinated entry diversion is already depleted.
Adding traditional congregate shelter beds does not address individuals with severe mental illness and substance use disorders who need pallet homes or non-congregate options.
Developers receiving affordable housing bond funds should be contractually linked to Continuum of Care referral lists.
conflicts.side_b_position: Demand longitudinal outcome data and accountability on eviction diversion before committing additional funds, and emphasize upstream prevention.
side_b_arguments: County eviction diversion is capped at $2,000 while families present with $8,000 in arrears, raising concerns that funds only delay eviction by a few months.
DSS currently treats requests as one-time aid and lacks data-sharing with Legal Aid on whether recipients are later evicted.
Decision-makers owe taxpayers full transparency on whether stabilization funds prevent long-term eviction.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; staff committed to pulling HUD recidivism benchmark reports, exploring Legal Aid data-sharing, and returning with formal FY26 HSAC budget requests and strategic plan options.

conflicts.issue: City-County Cost-Sharing for $120,000 Emergency Rental Assistance Shortfall and FY25 Eviction Diversion
conflicts.summary: City and County leaders disagreed over whether the City should split the emergency $120,000 DSS rental assistance shortfall 60/40 with the County given historical funding divisions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Split the urgent $120,000 FY24 gap proportionally—60% County ($72,000) and 40% City ($48,000)—aligned with property tax rate shares rather than leaving the County to cover an unbudgeted emergency alone.
side_a_arguments: Emergency funding needed between April and June 30 sits outside regular annual budget allocations.
Both jurisdictions face shared constituent eviction pressures and should share the bridge cost proportionately.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain the historical division in which the City funds Forever Home Durham ($8.2M dedicated tax) and Legal Aid eviction defense ($500k–$1M annually) while the County handles DSS rental assistance.
side_b_arguments: City Manager Wanda Page and Councilmember Javiera Caballero noted the City already commits major dedicated tax dollars to housing supply and tenant legal representation under a 2018/2019 division of labor.
Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton requested three concrete funding options before City Council takes up the request.
conflicts.resolution: No committee vote; staff was directed to present funding options for the City Council work session ahead of the County's April 22 regular meeting.

conflicts.issue: Administration of Rental Assistance: County DSS vs. Jointly Funded Standalone Nonprofit
conflicts.summary: Following DSS's update on eviction diversion funding and policy reforms, City Council Member Javiera Caballero suggested outsourcing rental assistance to a nonprofit, drawing strong pushback from County Commissioner Nimasheena Burns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Consider moving rental assistance out of County DSS into a jointly funded standalone nonprofit.
side_a_arguments: Residents often perceive barriers to seeking help at DSS, which previously led the City and County to hire care navigation teams during ERAP.
A dedicated nonprofit jointly funded by City and County could disburse rental assistance faster than government bureaucracy.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep eviction diversion within County DSS (unless strict joint rules are established) and ensure full transparency across City and County programs.
side_b_arguments: DSS ranked among the fastest jurisdictions in North Carolina and nationally in deploying HOPE/ERAP funds using pre-existing systems, and Legal Aid declined to take over program administration.
The City's past subcontracted nonprofit ERAP program still has unanswered public records requests regarding guidelines and households served, and the City had to return unspent ERAP dollars.
conflicts.resolution: County Commissioner Nimasheena Burns (along with DSS leadership) defended DSS retention while Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton noted City staff would respond to Burns's data queries; no structural change was adopted.

conflicts.issue: Structure of Joint Meetings Between the City, County, and DPS Board of Education
conflicts.summary: Committee members discussed whether to replace all Joint City-County meetings with three-body meetings including the DPS Board of Education or to retain separate bilateral meetings and convert only two sessions per year.
conflicts.side_a_position: Retain separate City-County and County-School Board meetings for distinct jurisdictional matters, and include the Board of Education in two joint sessions per year (February and August).
side_a_arguments: Many County-School Board budget discussions do not involve the City, and vice versa.
Bilateral County-School Board meetings are valuable for relationship-building.
Two targeted tripartite sessions (pre-budget in February and August) address shared infrastructure and transportation without adding extra meetings.
conflicts.side_b_position: Incorporate the Board of Education more regularly into existing joint meetings since residents expect unified responsiveness across all three bodies.
side_b_arguments: Residents often do not distinguish which elected body holds oversight for school, transit, and infrastructure issues.
Using existing City-County slots with staff already in the room is efficient and transparent.
More frequent three-way coordination may be needed between February and August.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved by consensus and unanimous vote to invite the DPS Board of Education to two scheduled 2025 meetings (February 11 and August 12) while keeping open the option to invite them to future sessions if issues arise.

conflicts.issue: School Impact Fees, Developer Proffers, and City-County Legislative Alignment on Growth Concurrency
conflicts.summary: Following DPS's projection of $480M+ in new school seat construction needs, elected officials and attorneys examined whether the City or County could require developer impact fees or concurrency while debating how to align joint lobbying in Raleigh.
conflicts.side_a_position: Questioned the legal basis prohibiting local school impact fees and suggested challenging infrastructure definitions and accepting City voluntary proffers while coordinating joint City-County lobbying.
side_a_arguments: School buildings are essential public infrastructure driven directly by residential rezonings.
The City has not faced legal claims over voluntary proffers accepted on behalf of the school system.
Joint City-County legislative alignment is needed in the upcoming General Assembly long session.
conflicts.side_b_position: Legal counsel advised that North Carolina's Dillon's Rule and the 2006 Durham Land Owners Association decision strictly prohibit county-mandated school impact fees or concurrency without state enabling legislation.
side_b_arguments: Under Dillon's Rule, counties lack statutory authority to impose school impact fees or taxes without General Assembly authorization.
Orange County / Chapel Hill had to reimburse developers after a lawsuit over adequate public facilities fees.
Only voluntary proffers or new state enabling legislation are legally viable.
conflicts.resolution: BOCC had already referred the issue to its legislative liaison (Deborah Craig-Ray) for County legislative goals, and Chair Nida Allam committed to placing a joint City-County legislative priorities alignment presentation on the next meeting agenda.

meetings.title: Joint City-County Committee Meeting Dec 10, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Dr. Mike Lee presided over the December 10, 2024 Joint City-County Committee meeting alongside Durham County Commissioners and Durham City Council members. The committee approved prior meeting minutes and adopted its 2025 meeting calendar with modifications to begin meetings at 9:30 AM and invite the Durham Public Schools Board of Education to participate in the February 11 and August 12 joint sessions. Members also received an update on the City-County-DPS Housing Task Force and heard an extensive joint presentation from City Community Development and County staff on homelessness data, shelter capacity shortfalls, eviction diversion depletion, and a proposed $2.4 million FY26 joint investment request.

agenda_items.title: Welcome, Opening Remarks, and Quorum Deferral
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Dr. Mike Lee opened the Joint City-County Committee meeting and noted a light agenda. Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton welcomed the newly elected County Commissioners and emphasized continued collaboration on housing and crime prevention. Because a quorum had not yet arrived, the committee deferred approval items until additional members joined.

agenda_items.title: Discussion of Replacing or Incorporating Joint City-County Meetings with the Board of Education
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Members debated a leadership-level proposal to include the Durham Public Schools Board of Education in Joint City-County meetings following Matthew Palmer's August presentation on synchronizing school capacity and development. Commissioner Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Michelle Burton argued against replacing all County-School Board meetings, proposing instead to convert two existing City-County dates per year (February and August) into tripartite sessions. City Council members Mark-Anthony Middleton and Javiera Caballero supported using existing calendar slots rather than adding more meetings, and Burton and Lee endorsed shifting the meeting start time to 9:30 AM to accommodate school drop-off schedules.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (June 11, 2024 and August 13, 2024)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Once a quorum was established at 00:23:02, Chair Dr. Mike Lee returned to the deferred approval of the June 11, 2024 and August 13, 2024 Joint City-County Committee meeting minutes. No corrections or objections were raised by members of either body.

agenda_items.title: Approval of 2025 Joint City-County Meeting Calendar
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Wendy Jacobs proposed amending the 2025 calendar to invite the DPS Board of Education to the February 11 and August 12 sessions to focus on shared infrastructure, transportation, and pre-budget coordination, noting August 12 was already slated as a joint County-School Board date. Commissioner Michelle Burton requested moving all 2025 meetings to 9:30 AM so parents could drop children at high schools before attending, and Councilwoman Javiera Caballero asked for flexibility to invite the school board to additional sessions if urgent needs arose. Legal counsel confirmed the modifications could be included in the approval motion.

agenda_items.title: Update on the City-County-DPS Housing Task Force
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Councilwoman Javiera Caballero reported that task force subcommittees—including gap financing, pre-shelter housing, homeless services, and land use—were nearing draft recommendations while awaiting a joint Housing Needs Assessment expected in late January or early February. Commissioner Wendy Jacobs inquired whether existing affordable housing units at risk of losing affordability protections, pipeline tracking, and diverse housing typologies were being evaluated. Commissioner Michelle Burton asked for baseline figures on the County's unhoused population, which staff deferred to the subsequent homeless services presentation.

agenda_items.title: Presentation on Homeless Services: Needs, Funding, and Solutions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Community Development Director Reginald Johnson, Homeless Manager Colin Davis, and County Special Projects Coordinator Samantha Smith presented a comprehensive breakdown of Durham's Continuum of Care, federal/local funding (~$4M City plus County shelter, outreach, Carver Creek, ARPA, and prevention investments), and rising unsheltered counts (172 unsheltered in the 2024 point-in-time count, with 51 families and 50 single adults waiting for emergency shelter). Davis outlined the Homeless Services Advisory Committee's proposed $2.4 million FY26 ask ($1.2M City for diversion, street outreach, and flexible housing subsidies; $1.2M County for expanded emergency/non-traditional shelter and a day center). Elected officials pressed staff on tracking set-aside units in bond-funded housing, severe mental illness/substance use gaps, non-congregate pallet homes, and impending mid-year depletion of County eviction diversion ($45,184 left) and Open Doors ($14,786 left) funds, with some members calling for stronger outcome tracking on rental assistance.

agenda_items.title: Next Meeting Reminder and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Dr. Mike Lee reminded members that the next meeting on February 11, 2025 would include the Durham Public Schools Board of Education. The committee then moved, seconded, and unanimously voted to adjourn.

votes.item_title: Approval of June 11, 2024 and August 13, 2024 Joint City-County Committee Minutes
votes.notes: Deferred from 00:15:12 until a quorum was established at 00:23:02. Joint committee includes both BOCC and Durham City Council members; individual roll-call attendance was not read.
votes.discussion_detail: At the start of the meeting at 00:15:12, Chair Dr. Mike Lee noted that the committee did not yet have a quorum and deferred action on the approval items until additional members arrived. After discussing the tripartite school board meeting proposal, a quorum was confirmed at 00:23:02. Chair Lee then returned to the approval of the June 11, 2024 and August 13, 2024 minutes that had been circulated in the agenda packet. No members offered corrections or discussion, and the motion passed unanimously by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Approval of 2025 Joint City-County Meeting Calendar (as Amended for DPS Participation and 9:30 AM Start Time)
votes.notes: Wendy Jacobs proposed inviting DPS to the February 11 and August 12 dates; Michelle Burton proposed the 9:30 AM start time; Chair Dr. Mike Lee restated the final amended motion at 00:28:16 and attorneys confirmed legal propriety.
votes.discussion_detail: Building on the preceding discussion of tripartite coordination, Commissioner Wendy Jacobs proposed inviting the Durham Public Schools Board of Education to the February 11 and August 12, 2025 meetings to address pre-budget, infrastructure, and transportation alignment without adding extra meetings to the calendar. The clerk noted that August 12 was already approved on the County calendar as a County-Board of Education meeting, making a three-body session efficient and avoiding a scheduling conflict. Commissioner Michelle Burton requested changing the meeting start time to 9:30 AM to accommodate parents dropping off high school students after 9:15 AM, which Chair Dr. Mike Lee supported. Following Councilwoman Javiera Caballero's request to retain flexibility to invite the school board to other sessions if needed and confirmation from legal counsel, Chair Lee restated the amended calendar motion, which passed unanimously by voice vote.

votes.notes: Joint City-County Committee adjournment following the homeless services presentation.
votes.discussion_detail: After concluding nearly two hours of discussion on homelessness services, shelter capacity, and eviction diversion funding, Chair Dr. Mike Lee asked for any final comments and reminded attendees that the next meeting on February 11, 2025 would include the Durham Public Schools Board of Education. Hearing no further business, Chair Lee solicited a motion to adjourn. A motion and second were made from the dais and approved unanimously by voice vote.

meetings.title: BOCC City Joint Meeting August 13, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Nida Allam convened the August 13, 2024 Joint City-County Committee meeting with Durham County Commissioners and Durham City Council members. Durham Public Schools Lead Planner Matthew Palmer presented 10-year enrollment forecasts showing an anticipated 4,800 additional students from over 200 approved or pending residential developments—pushing high school utilization to 118% and creating an estimated $480 million raw construction need at $100,000 per seat—which sparked discussion on North Carolina's legal ban on school impact fees and aligning City-County legislative priorities. Aging Well Durham Executive Director Shelisa Howard-Martinez then presented the updated five-year Durham Comprehensive Aging Plan and its 13 implementation goals, and the joint committee unanimously approved its prior minutes before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, and Land Acknowledgment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Nida Allam welcomed Durham City Council colleagues and County Commissioners to the joint meeting, read the public charge and land acknowledgment, and noted that minutes approval would be deferred until a quorum arrived.

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Synchronizing Enrollment, Capacity, and Residential Development (DPS)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Public Schools Lead Planner Matthew Palmer and Acting COO Dr. Todd LoFrese, alongside City-County Planning staff, presented a 10-year forecast projecting 4,800 additional DPS students generated by 200+ residential developments, pushing middle schools to 97% (Neal Middle to 119–120%) and high schools from 104% to 118% utilization against a 35,000-seat capacity, with raw construction estimated at $100,000 per seat. Palmer outlined state HB 90 K–3 class size caps and legal barriers under Dillon's Rule and the 2006 Durham Land Owners Association ruling barring county school impact fees and concurrency ordinances. Commissioners and council members discussed voluntary developer proffers, coordinating state/federal lobbying via the County's upcoming lobbyists, and adding a joint legislative-priorities alignment item to the next meeting.

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Aging Well Durham & Comprehensive Aging Plan Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Aging Well Durham Executive Director Shelisa Howard-Martinez presented the updated five-year Durham Comprehensive Aging Plan developed across nine livability domains—adding abuse, neglect, and exploitation while making communication crosscutting—and highlighted 13 three-year implementation goals aligned with City and County strategic priorities. Officials discussed rising homelessness among residents aged 50+, Aging in Place home modifications, permanent supportive housing, elder financial fraud and sweetheart scams, and establishing five-year evaluation metrics under the collective impact model.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Joint City-County Meeting Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Before Mayor Leonardo Williams had to depart, Chair Nida Allam confirmed with Clerk Monica Wallace that a quorum was present and entertained a motion to approve the minutes. Mayor Williams moved and Council Member Javiera Caballero seconded approval, passing unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Closing Remarks and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Nida Allam thanked Director Howard-Martinez and offered to coordinate with Mayor Leonardo Williams on whether to schedule the Aging Well Durham presentation for the full City Council before declaring the meeting adjourned.

votes.item_title: Approval of Joint City-County Committee Meeting Minutes
votes.notes: Joint City-County Committee vote; moved by City of Durham Mayor Leonardo Williams and seconded by Council Member Javiera Caballero once quorum was confirmed prior to the Mayor's departure.
votes.discussion_detail: At the start of the meeting at 00:14:35, Chair Nida Allam deferred action on the minutes because a formal quorum had not yet gathered. During the Q&A on the Aging Well Durham presentation at 01:43:04, Chair Allam paused because Mayor Leonardo Williams needed to leave and confirmed with Clerk Monica Wallace that a quorum was present to vote on the minutes. Mayor Williams moved to approve the minutes, Council Member Javiera Caballero seconded, and the motion passed unanimously by voice vote.

meetings.title: Joint City-County Meeting 6/11/2024
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council and Durham Board of County Commissioners held an informational Joint City-County meeting centered on workforce housing funding and a comprehensive review of gun violence and youth safety. The session opened with an update on the Chamber Foundation's revived interest in supporting workforce housing at an estimated level of around $300,000, followed by Mayor Leonardo Williams initiating a joint briefing from the Durham Police Department and Sheriff's Office in response to recent shootings, including a three-year-old shot the night before. Officials and law enforcement examined existing interventions (HEART, ShotSpotter, and Project BUILD, which operates on roughly $500,000 including $100,000 from the City and plans to expand to ages 10–13), alongside school mental health gaps, North Carolina gun laws, and juvenile justice challenges under the state's Raise the Age law (noting only 12 of 131 violent assaults in the prior year reached the juvenile justice level). No formal motions or votes were taken during the meeting.

agenda_items.title: Chamber Foundation Workforce Housing Funding Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Officials recognized the Chamber of Commerce and its newly chaired Chamber Foundation for reviving efforts to support local housing work, with specific interest in workforce housing. Participants noted an anticipated funding contribution of roughly $300,000, with no further questions or formal action.

agenda_items.title: Joint Briefing on Gun Violence, Youth Safety, and Law Enforcement Response
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams opened a policy discussion on gun violence following the shooting of a three-year-old the previous night and asked the Police Chief and Sheriff's Office for a high-level overview of current conditions and resources. Williams cited city tools including the violent harm reduction roundtable, Partners Against Crime, ShotSpotter, and the HEART team, while critiquing the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force for not addressing gun violence; another official urged stronger preventative funding in communities after the prior night's budget passage. Law enforcement and elected officials also discussed youth mental health requests from Hillside High School students, school counselor shortages, and North Carolina's comparatively permissive gun laws.

agenda_items.title: Juvenile Justice System, Pretrial Release, and Raise the Age Impacts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Officials and law enforcement examined juvenile crime prevention, pretrial release practices, and custody handoffs when juvenile detention declines intake and returns youth to working parents. Speakers reviewed North Carolina's Raise the Age law extending juvenile jurisdiction to age 18 and recent statutory remedies enabling adults who direct juveniles to commit crimes to be charged with the same offense. Data cited during the briefing indicated that out of 131 violent assaults in the prior year, only 12 reached the juvenile justice level.

agenda_items.title: Community Intervention and Support Services (Project BUILD) and Youth Mental Health
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Crystal, Director of Community Intervention and Support Services (overseeing BCU, Project BUILD, and MBK), discussed wraparound intervention services for referred youth. Officials noted Project BUILD operates on a budget around $500,000—including a $100,000 City contribution—for ages 14 to 21, with plans to expand to ages 10 to 13, while emphasizing rising mental health and trauma support needs before concluding the policy discussion.

agenda_items.title: Joint Meeting Scheduling and Closing Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Officials briefly discussed adjusting joint meeting scheduling and timing to prevent staff and district exhaustion before wrapping up the session without formal votes.

meetings.title: Joint City-County Committee Meeting Apr. 9, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the April 9, 2024 Joint City-County Committee meeting, elected officials and staff from Durham County and the City of Durham reviewed updates on the Combined City-County-DPS Housing Initiative, the Low-Income Homeowner Property Tax Relief (LIHR) program, the Durham Eviction Diversion / Rental Assistance program, and summer youth programming. The central policy clash focused on how to split an urgent $120,000 emergency eviction diversion shortfall for the remainder of FY24 and $1.3 million requested for FY25 between the City and County. Once a joint quorum was achieved late in the meeting, the committee unanimously approved its February 28, 2024 minutes.

agenda_items.title: Combined City-County-Durham Public Schools Housing Initiative Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Councilmember Javiera Caballero briefed the committee on efforts to unify City, County, and DPS housing efforts across short-, medium-, and long-term timelines, including subcommittees organized by AMI brackets and private philanthropic support for a housing needs assessment. Commissioner Wendy Jacobs recommended engaging the Durham Regional Association of Realtors in the planning process.

agenda_items.title: Low-Income Homeowner Property Tax Relief (LIHR) Program Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tax Administrator Keyar Dozier, DSS Director Maggie Cveticanin, and Assistant County Manager Dwayne Brinson presented performance metrics for the LIHR program serving homeowners below 80% AMI with five-year residency who do not receive existing state exemptions. Participation grew from 340 households in FY22 ($357,000) to 406 in FY23 ($578,000) and 539 applications to date in FY24 against a combined $1.25 million budget ($750,000 County, $500,000 City). Officials discussed easing annual reapplication burdens, flaws in the state circuit breaker deferment program, and outreach ahead of the 2025 property tax revaluation.

agenda_items.title: Durham Eviction Diversion and Emergency Rental Assistance Funding Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DSS Director Maggie Cveticanin and staff member Megan Russ reported that DSS eviction-prevention rental assistance had exhausted its annual funds roughly one month earlier, requiring a $30,000 emergency transfer from Open Doors ($10,000 already spent between April 1 and April 8). Staff requested $120,000 in immediate emergency funding to cover needs through June 30 and $1.3 million for FY25. City and County representatives debated cost-sharing responsibilities, with County leaders proposing a 60/40 split for the emergency ask while City officials cited Forever Home Durham and City-funded Legal Aid eviction defense.

agenda_items.title: Approval of February 28, 2024 Joint City-County Committee Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns having joined earlier at 00:53:24 to establish a full committee quorum, Chair Allam brought forward the February 28, 2024 minutes, which were deferred at the start of the meeting. The committee approved the minutes unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Summer Youth Programming Activities Memo
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Officials briefly reviewed a written memo on summer programming from the Office on Youth in the absence of staff lead Ms. Khalil. Commissioner Jacobs, Vice Chair Burns, and City Manager Wanda Page emphasized improving youth participation tracking and centralizing program information on a shared website and listserv.

votes.item_title: Approval of February 28, 2024 Joint City-County Committee Minutes
votes.notes: Joint committee body included both City Councilmembers (Williams, Middleton, Caballero, Rist) and County Commissioners (Allam, Burns, Jacobs); individual roll call was not taken.
votes.discussion_detail: Approval of the February 28, 2024 Joint City-County Committee minutes was deferred at 00:17:46 because a full joint quorum had not yet arrived. After Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns joined the meeting at 00:53:24 and the committee concluded its eviction diversion discussion, Chair Nida Allam returned to the deferred minutes. Durham Mayor Leonardo Williams moved to approve the minutes and Vice Chair Burns seconded. All present City and County committee members voted aye unanimously by voice vote.

disagreements.issue: City-County Cost-Sharing for $120,000 Emergency Rental Assistance Shortfall and FY25 Eviction Diversion
disagreements.summary: City and County leaders disagreed over whether the City should split the emergency $120,000 DSS rental assistance shortfall 60/40 with the County given historical funding divisions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Split the urgent $120,000 FY24 gap proportionally—60% County ($72,000) and 40% City ($48,000)—aligned with property tax rate shares rather than leaving the County to cover an unbudgeted emergency alone.
side_a_arguments: Emergency funding needed between April and June 30 sits outside regular annual budget allocations.
Both jurisdictions face shared constituent eviction pressures and should share the bridge cost proportionately.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain the historical division in which the City funds Forever Home Durham ($8.2M dedicated tax) and Legal Aid eviction defense ($500k–$1M annually) while the County handles DSS rental assistance.
side_b_arguments: City Manager Wanda Page and Councilmember Javiera Caballero noted the City already commits major dedicated tax dollars to housing supply and tenant legal representation under a 2018/2019 division of labor.
Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton requested three concrete funding options before City Council takes up the request.
disagreements.resolution: No committee vote; staff was directed to present funding options for the City Council work session ahead of the County's April 22 regular meeting.

meetings.title: Joint City County Meeting Feb 28 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 28, 2024 Joint City-County meeting (presided over for the first time by Mayor Leonardo Williams), City Council and Durham County Commissioners approved the December 12 joint meeting minutes by unanimous voice vote and discussed three major interjurisdictional initiatives. The Environmental Affairs Board presented local climate hazard projections and urged forming a joint City-County-DPS resilience task force, Javiera Caballero introduced a Tri-Board Housing Initiative with Durham Public Schools, and DSS leaders warned that eviction diversion funds would run out by the end of February without a $320,000 bridge through June and $1.3M annually thereafter. Elected officials clashed over whether to shift rental assistance from DSS to a nonprofit and whether to reallocate unspent Low-Income Homeowner Relief Grant funds to cover the eviction diversion shortfall.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Draft Joint City-County Meeting Minutes (December 12, 2023)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the meeting to order at 9:08 a.m. and waited for quorum before presenting the draft December 12 Joint City-County meeting minutes prepared by the County Clerk.

agenda_items.title: Planning for Climate Change — Environmental Affairs Board Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: EAB Chair Jen Carrigan and Central Pines Regional Council coordinator Langston Alexander warned that Durham faces rising extreme heat (~45 days/year over 95°F), localized flooding, and drought, and recommended creating a joint task force to produce a Durham Community Resilience Plan by 2026. Council members and County Commissioners discussed PFAS water contamination, solar resilience hubs at Durham Public Schools, eastern NC climate migration, and the Person County power plant's impacts on Bahama and Rougemont wells, agreeing that Mayor Williams and BOCC Chair Nida Allam would consult managers on task force structure and FY25 funding.

agenda_items.title: Joint City-County-DPS Tri-Board Housing Initiative
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero (working with Housing for New Hope's Russell Pierce) proposed convening a cross-sector City, County, and DPS housing working group with employers, philanthropy, DHA, DHIC, and transit/planning staff to map land, gaps, and workforce/senior housing needs as Forever Home Durham and ARPA funds wind down. Mayor Williams, BOCC Chair Nida Allam, and DPS Chair Bettina Umstead agreed to sign a joint invitation letter launching the 20-25 member effort.

agenda_items.title: Eviction Diversion Funding Cliff and Program Updates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DSS Director Maggie Chotas and Program Manager Megan Rush reported that federal ERAP/NC Pro funds ran out in January 2024 following record December filings, leaving county eviction diversion funds (~$151,990) depleted by month-end and requiring $320,000 through June 2024 and $1.3M/year thereafter. Staff proposed waiving sustainability checks within 30 days of job loss, helping tenants two months behind before court filings, and partnering with Legal Aid, sparking debate over nonprofit administration and reallocating unspent Low-Income Homeowner Relief funds.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Referred to City and County Managers

votes.item_title: Approve Draft Joint City-County Meeting Minutes (December 12, 2023)
votes.notes: Joint vote of Durham City Council and Durham County BOCC; six City Council members were present at 00:43:28 (DeDreana Freeman arrived later at 00:59:41 due to a family hospital visit).
votes.discussion_detail: Opening the February 28, 2024 Joint City-County meeting, Mayor Leonardo Williams waited briefly for a quorum before bringing forward Item 1, the draft minutes of the December 12 Joint City-County meeting prepared by the County Clerk. Without debate or proposed corrections, a motion to approve the minutes was made and seconded. The joint bodies approved the minutes unanimously by voice vote.

disagreements.issue: Administration of Rental Assistance: County DSS vs. Jointly Funded Standalone Nonprofit
disagreements.summary: Following DSS's update on eviction diversion funding and policy reforms, City Council Member Javiera Caballero suggested outsourcing rental assistance to a nonprofit, drawing strong pushback from County Commissioner Nimasheena Burns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Consider moving rental assistance out of County DSS into a jointly funded standalone nonprofit.
side_a_arguments: Residents often perceive barriers to seeking help at DSS, which previously led the City and County to hire care navigation teams during ERAP.
A dedicated nonprofit jointly funded by City and County could disburse rental assistance faster than government bureaucracy.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep eviction diversion within County DSS (unless strict joint rules are established) and ensure full transparency across City and County programs.
side_b_arguments: DSS ranked among the fastest jurisdictions in North Carolina and nationally in deploying HOPE/ERAP funds using pre-existing systems, and Legal Aid declined to take over program administration.
The City's past subcontracted nonprofit ERAP program still has unanswered public records requests regarding guidelines and households served, and the City had to return unspent ERAP dollars.
disagreements.resolution: County Commissioner Nimasheena Burns (along with DSS leadership) defended DSS retention while Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton noted City staff would respond to Burns's data queries; no structural change was adopted.

disagreements.issue: Reallocating Unspent Low-Income Homeowner Relief Grant Funds to Eviction Diversion
disagreements.summary: Officials debated a County proposal to bridge the $320,000 eviction diversion shortfall by tapping unspent funds in the joint $1.2M Low-Income Homeowner Relief Grant program ($700K County / $500K City).
disagreements.side_a_position: Consider reallocating underutilized Low-Income Homeowner Relief Grant dollars to stabilize eviction diversion immediately.
side_a_arguments: Roughly $1.2M was allocated to homeowner relief with only ~$400K+ spent across two years, leaving idle funds on the table while eviction diversion runs out of money this month.
Moving unused ('lazy') funds in an acute housing crisis is sound fiscal practice and does not preclude replenishing homeowner relief later if needed.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not pit low-income homeowners against renters or reduce homeowner relief funds ahead of the upcoming property tax revaluation; fix application barriers instead.
side_b_arguments: Cutting homeowner relief ahead of next year's property tax revaluation risks harming vulnerable homeowners; the program is underutilized because the application process is clunky and needs streamlining.
Other funding sources should be identified to cover the $320,000 gap and $1.3M annual need.
disagreements.resolution: Mayor Leonardo Williams agreed to meet with BOCC Chair Nida Allam and both the City and County Managers to identify the best funding mechanism without an immediate vote.
